title: Architecture Decision Records in Practice
objectives: Use ADRs to capture, communicate and defend architecture decisions
Write ADRs that honestly present context, options and trade-offs
Determine when a decision warrants an ADR and when it does not
Manage the ADR lifecycle from proposed through to superseded
Apply ADRs effectively in government contexts including spend controls and assessments
whyThisMatters:
Every architecture is the sum of its decisions. The technology choices, the integration patterns, the trade-offs accepted, the options rejected. Yet in most government programmes, these decisions exist only in the memories of the people who made them. When those people move on, which they always do in the civil service, the reasoning disappears. New teams inherit systems they do not understand, repeat mistakes that were already made, and reverse decisions without knowing why they were made in the first place.

Architecture Decision Records solve this problem simply and cheaply. An ADR is a short document that captures a single architecture decision: the context, the options considered, the decision made, and the consequences. It takes 20 minutes to write. It saves weeks of confusion later. It provides an audit trail for spend controls and service assessments. It gives new team members a way to understand not just what the system is, but why it is that way.

The reason this lesson matters now, after the documentation lesson, is that ADRs are the most practical form of architecture documentation you will ever use. They are short enough to write, specific enough to be useful, and structured enough to be findable. If you do nothing else from the previous lesson, do this: start writing ADRs. Your future self, your future colleagues, and your future assessors will thank you.

content.heading: What ADRs Are and Why They Matter
content.body:
An Architecture Decision Record is a short document that captures a single significant architecture decision. The concept was popularised by Michael Nygard in 2011, and it has since become one of the most widely adopted practices in software architecture, including across UK government.

The core idea is simple: when you make a decision that is significant, hard to reverse, or likely to be questioned later, write it down in a structured format. Not in a meeting note that will be lost. Not in a Slack message that will scroll away. Not in your head where it will leave when you do. In a dedicated, findable, structured record.

ADRs matter for several reasons. First, they create institutional memory. Government programmes run for years. Staff rotate every 18 to 24 months on average. Without written records, every rotation loses knowledge. ADRs preserve the reasoning so that new team members can understand the system without archaeology.

Second, they improve decision quality. The act of writing down your reasoning forces you to think it through properly. If you cannot articulate why you chose Option A over Option B in writing, you probably have not thought about it carefully enough. The discipline of writing sharpens thinking.

Third, they provide an audit trail. In government, decisions about technology spending are subject to scrutiny. Spend controls, service assessments, internal audit, National Audit Office reviews. ADRs give you a clear, dated record of what was decided, by whom, and why. This is not bureaucracy. It is professional accountability.

Fourth, they enable honest disagreement. When a decision is captured in an ADR with its full context and trade-offs, people can disagree with it constructively. They can say 'the context has changed since this decision was made' or 'there is a new option that was not available then.' Without the record, disagreements become personal rather than professional.

content.heading: The Anatomy of a Good ADR
content.body:
A good ADR follows a consistent structure. There are several templates available, but the most effective for government use contains these sections:

Title: A short, descriptive name that makes the decision findable. Use the format 'ADR-NNN: Use PostgreSQL for the applicant data store' rather than 'ADR-NNN: Database decision.' The title should tell you what was decided without opening the document.

Status: The current state of the decision. Typically one of: Proposed, Accepted, Deprecated, Superseded. This tells readers whether the decision is still active.

Date: When the decision was made (or proposed). This matters because context changes over time. A decision made in 2021 may have been correct then but need revisiting now.

Context: The situation that prompted the decision. What problem were you solving? What constraints existed? What had already been decided that shaped your options? This section should be honest and specific. Include the political and organisational context, not just the technical context. In government, decisions are shaped by procurement timelines, spending review cycles, ministerial priorities, and cross-departmental dependencies. Capture these.

Options Considered: The alternatives you evaluated. For each option, briefly describe what it involves and its key advantages and disadvantages. Be honest about all options, including the one you chose. Do not present rejected options as straw men.

Decision: What you decided. State it clearly in one or two sentences. If the decision has conditions or caveats, state those too.

Consequences: What follows from this decision. What becomes easier? What becomes harder? What risks have you accepted? What will you need to revisit? What other decisions does this force or enable? This section is where you demonstrate that you have thought through the implications, not just the immediate choice.

Optionally, you might include: Decision Makers (who was involved), Related ADRs (what other decisions connect to this one), and Review Date (when this decision should be reconsidered).

content.heading: When to Write an ADR (and When Not To)
content.body:
Not every decision needs an ADR. Writing too many dilutes their value and creates maintenance overhead. Writing too few means important reasoning is lost. The skill is knowing where the threshold sits.

Write an ADR when the decision is significant and hard to reverse. Choosing your primary database technology, your hosting platform, your integration pattern, your authentication approach: these are ADR-worthy decisions. They shape the system for months or years. Reversing them is expensive.

Write an ADR when the decision will be questioned later. If you can predict that someone will ask 'why did we do it this way?' in six months, write the ADR now while the reasoning is fresh. In government, this includes any decision that might be questioned at a spend control, service assessment, or audit.

Write an ADR when there is genuine disagreement. If the team debated the decision, capture the debate. The ADR preserves the reasoning for both sides and records how the disagreement was resolved. This prevents the same argument recurring every few months.

Write an ADR when the decision affects multiple teams. If your decision constrains or enables other teams' work, they need to understand why. An ADR gives them the context without requiring a meeting.

Do NOT write an ADR for standard, obvious, or trivial decisions. If your department has a standard CI/CD pipeline and you are using it unchanged, that does not need an ADR. If you are choosing between two equivalent libraries for JSON parsing, that does not need an ADR. If the decision can be easily reversed in a day's work, it probably does not need an ADR.

Do NOT write an ADR for implementation details. The choice between a for loop and a map function is not architecture. The choice between two equivalent ways of structuring a module is not architecture. ADRs are for decisions that shape the system at a structural level.

A useful heuristic: if the decision would appear in a solution architecture document, it probably warrants an ADR. If it would only appear in a code review comment, it probably does not.

content.heading: Capturing Context and Options Honestly
content.body:
The most common failure in ADRs is dishonesty. Not deliberate lying, but the unconscious tendency to present the chosen option as obviously correct and the rejected options as obviously flawed. This undermines the entire purpose of the ADR.

Honest context means capturing the real situation, including the uncomfortable parts. If you chose a particular vendor because the procurement framework limited your options, say so. If you chose a simpler architecture because the team lacked the skills for a more sophisticated one, say so. If you chose a more expensive option because the timeline did not allow for the cheaper alternative, say so. Future readers need to understand the real constraints, not an idealised version.

Honest options means presenting each alternative fairly. Every option you considered had advantages, or you would not have considered it. State those advantages clearly, even for the options you rejected. Similarly, the option you chose has disadvantages. State those too. An ADR that presents the chosen option as having no downsides is not credible.

Here is what dishonest options look like: Option A (the one we chose) described as modern, scalable, well-supported, cost-effective, aligns with strategy. Option B described as legacy technology, expensive, does not scale, vendor lock-in. Option C described as immature, risky, no government precedent. This is advocacy, not analysis.

Here is what honest options look like: Option A (managed cloud service) with advantages of lower operational overhead, automatic scaling, strong vendor support, and disadvantages of higher unit cost at current volumes, limited customisation, creates dependency on a single cloud provider. Option B (self-hosted open source) with advantages of lower licensing cost, full control over configuration, no vendor lock-in, and disadvantages of requiring a dedicated operations team we do not currently have, scaling requires manual intervention, support depends on community. Option C (emerging platform) with advantages of best technical fit for the specific use case, lowest long-term cost projections, and disadvantages of limited production track record, small vendor with financial risk, no existing government adoption to reference.

The second version is useful. It tells future readers what the real trade-offs were. It allows them to reassess if the context changes. It demonstrates professional rigour to assessors and auditors.

content.heading: The Status Lifecycle
content.body:
ADRs are not static documents. They have a lifecycle that reflects the reality of architecture decisions in long-running programmes.

Proposed: The decision has been drafted but not yet accepted. This status is useful when you want to circulate a decision for review before committing to it. In government, where decisions often need sign-off from multiple stakeholders, the Proposed status gives people time to challenge before the decision becomes official.

Accepted: The decision has been agreed and is in effect. This is the normal active state. The system is being built or operated according to this decision.

Deprecated: The decision is still technically in effect but is no longer the recommended approach. New work should not follow this decision, but existing implementations do not need to change immediately. This status is common in government where legacy decisions coexist with newer approaches during transition periods.

Superseded: The decision has been replaced by a newer decision. The ADR should link to its replacement. The old ADR is preserved for historical context, showing how thinking evolved over time. Never delete superseded ADRs. They are part of the decision history.

Some teams add additional statuses like Rejected (proposed but not accepted) or Under Review (being reconsidered). Keep it simple. The four core statuses cover most situations.

The key discipline is updating status when it changes. A common failure is leaving ADRs in Accepted status long after the decision has been superseded. This confuses new team members who find contradictory active decisions. When you make a new decision that changes an old one, update both ADRs in the same commit or the same day.

In government programmes that run for years, you will accumulate dozens of ADRs. Some will be superseded multiple times. This is normal and healthy. It shows that architecture is evolving in response to changing context, not frozen in an initial design that no longer fits.

content.heading: Storing and Discovering ADRs
content.body:
Where you store ADRs matters as much as what you write in them. If people cannot find them, they do not exist.

The strongest approach is storing ADRs in the same version control repository as the code they relate to. This has several advantages: they are versioned alongside the code, they appear in pull requests when decisions change, they are discoverable by anyone with access to the repository, and they benefit from the same review process as code changes.

A typical structure is a docs/adr or docs/architecture/decisions directory in the repository root, with files named sequentially: 0001-use-postgresql-for-applicant-data.md, 0002-adopt-event-driven-integration.md, and so on. The sequential numbering provides a chronological record. The descriptive filename makes each decision findable without opening the file.

For programmes with multiple repositories, you have a choice: store ADRs in each repository (for decisions specific to that component) and maintain a central repository for cross-cutting decisions that affect the whole platform. This mirrors how decisions actually work: some are local, some are global.

Confluence, SharePoint, and other wiki-style tools are less ideal for ADRs because they lack version control, make it harder to link decisions to code changes, and tend to become disorganised over time. However, if your team already uses Confluence and will not adopt repository-based documentation, Confluence ADRs are better than no ADRs. Pragmatism beats purity.

Discoverability is critical. New team members need to find relevant ADRs without reading all of them. Useful approaches include: a table of contents file (an index listing all ADRs with their status and a one-line summary), consistent tagging or categorisation, and cross-references between related ADRs. Some teams generate an ADR index automatically from the file metadata.

In government, where staff rotate frequently, the first thing a new architect should do when joining a programme is read the ADR index. It gives them a compressed history of every significant decision and why it was made. Twenty minutes of reading saves weeks of asking questions and making assumptions.

content.heading: ADRs in Government: Spend Controls, Assessments and Audit
content.body:
ADRs have particular value in UK government because of the governance and assurance landscape that surrounds technology decisions.

Spend controls require departments to justify significant technology spending to the Central Digital and Data Office (CDDO). When you submit a spend control request, you need to demonstrate that you have considered alternatives, made rational choices, and understood the implications. A set of well-written ADRs provides exactly this evidence. Instead of writing a retrospective justification for the spend control panel, you can point to decisions made in real time with full context. This is more credible and less effort.

Service assessments evaluate whether a service meets the Service Standard. Assessors look for evidence of good architecture decision-making: that options were considered, that trade-offs were understood, that decisions align with the Technology Code of Practice. ADRs are the most direct evidence you can provide. An assessor who can read your ADRs and understand your reasoning will have far more confidence in your architecture than one who has to extract this information through questioning.

Internal audit and the National Audit Office occasionally review technology programmes, particularly those that have overspent or underdelivered. When this happens, having a clear decision trail is invaluable. ADRs show that decisions were made deliberately, with appropriate consideration, at identifiable points in time. The alternative, reconstructing decision history from memory and meeting notes months or years later, is painful and unreliable.

There is also a defensive value. In government, decisions are sometimes challenged politically. A minister asks why a particular technology was chosen. A select committee questions the cost. A Freedom of Information request asks for the rationale. ADRs give you a clear, professional answer that was written at the time of the decision, not constructed after the fact.

The practical implication: treat ADRs as a professional habit, not as documentation overhead. They protect you, your team, and your programme. The 20 minutes you spend writing an ADR today could save you days of retrospective justification later.

content.heading: Common Mistakes and Lightweight vs Heavyweight Approaches
content.body:
Having advocated for ADRs, let me be honest about how they go wrong.

The most common mistake is writing ADRs that are too long. An ADR should be one to two pages. If it is longer, you are probably trying to capture too much in a single record. Split it into multiple decisions or move detailed analysis into a separate options paper that the ADR references.

The second mistake is writing ADRs after the fact. A retrospective ADR is better than nothing, but it loses the honesty of real-time capture. When you write an ADR weeks after the decision, you unconsciously rationalise. You forget the options you briefly considered and dismissed. You present the outcome as more inevitable than it was. Write ADRs at the time of the decision, or as close to it as possible.

The third mistake is treating ADRs as approvals rather than records. An ADR records a decision. It is not a change request form that requires six signatures. If your ADR process requires formal approval from multiple governance boards before a decision can be recorded, you have turned a lightweight practice into a heavyweight process and teams will stop using it.

The fourth mistake is never updating status. Superseded ADRs that still show as Accepted confuse everyone. Make status updates part of your decision-making process: when you make a new decision, check whether it supersedes an existing one.

The fifth mistake is inconsistent adoption. If only some decisions get ADRs, people cannot trust that the ADR set is complete. They still have to ask 'was there an ADR for this?' rather than knowing that all significant decisions are captured. Consistency matters more than perfection.

On the lightweight versus heavyweight spectrum: start lightweight. A simple markdown template with Title, Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences is enough. You can add sections (Options Considered, Decision Makers, Review Date) as your practice matures. But start simple. A team that writes simple ADRs consistently is better off than a team that has a perfect template but rarely uses it because it feels like too much work.

The goal is a sustainable practice that becomes habit, not a documentation burden that people resent. If writing an ADR takes more than 30 minutes, something is wrong. Either the decision is too complex for a single ADR (split it) or you are over-thinking the format (simplify it).

workedExample.title: DWP Universal Credit Platform Migration Decision
workedExample.context: The Department for Work and Pensions is migrating components of the Universal Credit platform from an on-premises data centre to cloud hosting. The architecture team needs to decide on the integration pattern for connecting the migrated cloud components with the legacy systems that will remain on-premises for the next three years. This decision affects 14 development teams, involves sensitive personal data (benefit claims, income details, health information), and must maintain 99.9% availability for a service that 6 million people depend on.
workedExample.approach:
The Lead Solution Architect writes an ADR capturing the decision. Here is how they approach it:

First, they capture the real context honestly. The context section notes not just the technical situation (hybrid cloud/on-premises environment) but also the organisational constraints: the programme has committed to a cloud migration timeline that cannot slip because it is tied to a data centre exit contract with financial penalties. The security team has concerns about data traversing the public internet. The development teams have varying levels of cloud experience. The existing integration uses a proprietary enterprise service bus that the vendor is end-of-lifing.

Second, they present three genuine options:

Option 1: API Gateway with mutual TLS over dedicated network link. Advantages: familiar pattern, strong security posture, works with existing team skills. Disadvantages: single point of failure, requires dedicated network provisioning (8-week lead time), creates bottleneck for all cross-environment traffic.

Option 2: Event-driven integration using managed message broker. Advantages: decoupled, resilient to temporary outages, scales independently. Disadvantages: requires significant rework of existing synchronous integrations, team needs training, eventual consistency model requires careful handling for financial transactions.

Option 3: Service mesh with sidecar proxies spanning both environments. Advantages: transparent to applications, provides observability, handles routing automatically. Disadvantages: operational complexity, immature in hybrid scenarios, limited government precedent, requires specialist skills the team does not have.

Third, they state the decision clearly: 'We will adopt Option 1 (API Gateway with mutual TLS) for the initial migration phase, with a planned transition to Option 2 (event-driven) for new integrations once the team has completed training and the first three services have migrated successfully.'

Fourth, they document the consequences honestly: this means the first migrated services will have a dependency on the dedicated network link. If that link fails, those services fail. This risk is accepted because the alternative (delaying migration for event-driven rework) would breach the data centre exit timeline. The transition to event-driven integration is planned for Q3, and a separate ADR will be written when that decision is confirmed.
workedExample.outcome: The ADR is reviewed by the technical leadership team and accepted. Six months later, when a new architect joins and questions why the API Gateway pattern was chosen over event-driven (which they consider superior), the ADR provides the full context. They can see it was a pragmatic decision driven by timeline constraints and team readiness, not ignorance of better patterns. They can also see that the transition to event-driven was always planned. This prevents an unnecessary debate and allows the new architect to focus on executing the planned transition rather than relitigating the original decision.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The ADR's value was not in the decision itself, which was relatively straightforward given the constraints. The value was in capturing the constraints honestly (especially the data centre exit penalty and team skill gaps), presenting the phased approach explicitly, and creating a record that prevented future teams from misunderstanding the reasoning. The 25 minutes spent writing the ADR saved at least two meetings worth of re-explanation when new team members joined over the following year.

civilServiceScenario.title: Ministry of Justice Digital Case Management Platform
civilServiceScenario.background: The Ministry of Justice is building a new digital case management platform to replace five separate legacy systems used across different court jurisdictions. The programme is in beta phase with 8 development teams working across multiple repositories. Architecture decisions have been made verbally in meetings and recorded inconsistently in Confluence pages, Slack threads, and email chains. A recent service assessment raised concerns that 'architecture decisions are not clearly documented or traceable.' The programme has also received a spend control condition requiring evidence of rational technology choices before the next tranche of funding is released.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You need to establish an ADR practice across 8 teams, retrospectively capture the 15-20 most significant decisions already made, and create a decision trail that satisfies both the service assessment panel and the spend control condition. The teams are mid-delivery and resistant to new processes. Some decisions were made months ago and the original decision-makers have moved to other programmes.
constraints: Eight development teams with different working practices and tooling
Spend control condition requiring evidence of rational technology choices within 6 weeks
Service assessment follow-up in 10 weeks expecting improved decision documentation
Key decision-makers for early decisions have left the programme
Teams are mid-sprint and resistant to new documentation overhead
Decisions span multiple repositories with no central architecture documentation
Some early decisions are now being questioned by newer team members
Budget for the next phase depends on satisfying the spend control condition
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Lead Solution Architect responsible for architecture governance across the programme. You have a small architecture team of two other SAs who can help, but the development teams report to delivery managers, not to you.
civilServiceScenario.discussion: This scenario tests your ability to introduce a practice pragmatically under time pressure. You cannot mandate ADRs and expect compliance. You need to demonstrate value quickly. Consider starting with the retrospective ADRs for the most significant decisions, because these satisfy the immediate governance needs. Write them yourself based on available evidence (meeting notes, Confluence pages, Slack history, conversations with remaining team members). Accept that retrospective ADRs will be less complete than real-time ones, but they are better than nothing. For the ongoing practice, make it as lightweight as possible. Provide a simple template. Offer to pair with developers on their first ADR. Show how ADRs reduce the number of 'why did we do this?' conversations. Make it easy to do the right thing rather than mandating compliance.

practiceArtefact.description: Write a complete ADR for the following decision: The Ministry of Justice case management platform needs to choose an authentication and identity approach for court staff, legal professionals, and citizens accessing the system. Write ADR-007: Authentication and Identity Strategy, considering the constraints of the government context (integration with GOV.UK One Login for citizens, existing departmental Active Directory for staff, Law Society credentials for solicitors).
practiceArtefact.guidance: Your ADR should follow the standard structure: Title, Status, Date, Context, Options Considered, Decision, and Consequences. Make the context specific and honest, including government constraints like the mandate to use GOV.UK One Login for citizen-facing services. Present at least three genuine options with fair advantages and disadvantages for each. State your decision clearly and explain the consequences, including what risks you are accepting and what future decisions this enables or forces. Keep the total length to one to two pages. Remember: this is a government system handling sensitive legal information, so security and data protection constraints are significant.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
ADR-007: Authentication and Identity Strategy for Case Management Platform

Status: Accepted

Date: 2024-03-15

Context:

The case management platform serves three distinct user populations with different identity needs:

1. Citizens (claimants, defendants, witnesses) who need to access case information, submit documents, and track progress. Government policy mandates GOV.UK One Login for citizen-facing services.

2. Court staff and MoJ employees who access the system through departmental devices. They have existing Active Directory identities managed by MoJ IT.

3. Legal professionals (solicitors, barristers, legal aid providers) who are external to MoJ but need authenticated access to case materials. Some have Law Society or Bar Council credentials.

The platform must handle OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE data including criminal records, family court proceedings, and financial information. Access control must be granular: a solicitor should see only their client's cases, not all cases.

The existing legacy systems use a mix of username/password authentication (for external users) and Windows Integrated Authentication (for staff). These approaches do not meet current security standards and cannot support the cross-jurisdiction access the new platform requires.

Constraints: Must integrate with GOV.UK One Login (government mandate). Must support MFA for all user types. Must achieve OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE security posture. Must not require legal professionals to obtain government-issued credentials.

Options Considered:

Option 1: Single identity provider for all users (GOV.UK One Login for everyone). Advantages: single integration point, consistent user experience, government-supported service. Disadvantages: GOV.UK One Login is designed for citizens, not professional users; does not support organisational identity federation; would require legal professionals to create personal government accounts rather than using professional credentials; does not integrate with MoJ Active Directory for staff.

Option 2: Federated identity with separate providers per user type. GOV.UK One Login for citizens, Azure AD (connected to MoJ Active Directory) for staff, and a dedicated identity broker for legal professionals that accepts Law Society and Bar Council credentials. Advantages: each user type authenticates through their natural identity provider; supports existing credentials; enables granular access control per user type. Disadvantages: three integration points to maintain; complexity in the authorisation layer mapping different identity claims to platform permissions; requires building or procuring the legal professional identity broker.

Option 3: Custom-built identity platform. Advantages: full control over user experience and features; can be tailored exactly to requirements. Disadvantages: significant build and maintenance cost; duplicates capability available from existing services; security risk of building authentication from scratch; contrary to Technology Code of Practice principle of reusing existing services.

Decision:

We will adopt Option 2: Federated identity with GOV.UK One Login for citizens, Azure AD for MoJ staff, and a dedicated identity broker for legal professionals. The legal professional broker will initially accept Law Society digital certificates and username/password with MFA, with Bar Council federation added in a later phase.

Consequences:

The platform's authorisation layer must handle identity claims from three different providers and map them to a unified permission model. This adds complexity to the access control design. We accept a dependency on GOV.UK One Login's roadmap for citizen authentication features. The legal professional identity broker is a new component that requires procurement or build. A separate ADR (ADR-008) will address the build vs buy decision for this component. Staff authentication benefits from existing MoJ security controls (device management, conditional access policies) without additional platform work. We accept the risk that GOV.UK One Login may not support all citizen journey requirements at launch; fallback to a simpler authentication flow may be needed for the private beta. This decision enables future integration with other justice system platforms (LAA, HMCTS Online) that also use federated identity.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about a significant architecture decision on your current or recent project. Could you explain why that decision was made if someone asked you in six months? Is the reasoning written down anywhere findable?
How many architecture decisions on your current programme exist only in people's memories? What would happen if those people left tomorrow?
When was the last time you changed an architecture decision? Did you update any documentation to reflect the change, or does the old decision still appear as current somewhere?

Think about a decision you disagreed with but accepted. If you had written an ADR at the time capturing the trade-offs honestly, would it be easier to revisit that decision now that context has changed?
How would your team react if you introduced ADRs tomorrow? What resistance would you expect, and how would you demonstrate value quickly enough to overcome it?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary purpose of an Architecture Decision Record?
options: To get formal approval for architecture decisions from governance boards
To capture the context, reasoning and consequences of a significant architecture decision
To document the complete technical specification of a system component
To assign responsibility for architecture decisions to specific individuals
knowledgeCheck.explanation: An ADR captures a single significant decision with its context, the options considered, the decision made, and the consequences. It is a record of reasoning, not an approval mechanism or a technical specification.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which of the following decisions would most appropriately warrant an ADR?
options: Choosing between two equivalent JSON parsing libraries
Deciding to use an event-driven integration pattern instead of synchronous API calls
Selecting the indentation style for the codebase
Choosing which developer will implement a particular feature
knowledgeCheck.explanation: ADRs are for significant, hard-to-reverse decisions that shape the system at a structural level. Choosing an integration pattern affects the entire system architecture and is difficult to reverse. Library choices, code style, and task assignment are not architecture decisions.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does it mean when an ADR has a status of 'Superseded'?
options: The decision was proposed but rejected by the governance board
The decision has been replaced by a newer decision, but the old ADR is preserved for historical context
The decision is still valid but needs to be reviewed soon
The decision was made incorrectly and should be ignored
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Superseded means the decision has been replaced by a newer one. The old ADR is kept as part of the decision history, showing how thinking evolved. It should link to the ADR that replaced it. Superseded ADRs are never deleted because they provide valuable historical context.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most effective place to store ADRs for a development team?
options: In a shared email folder accessible to all team members
In the same version control repository as the code they relate to
In a locked PDF document on the programme SharePoint
In the minutes of the architecture review board meetings
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Storing ADRs in the code repository means they are versioned alongside the code, discoverable by anyone with repository access, included in pull requests when decisions change, and benefit from the same review processes as code. This keeps them close to the work and maintained as part of normal development workflow.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why are ADRs particularly valuable in UK government technology programmes?
options: They are mandated by the Technology Code of Practice
They provide evidence for spend controls, service assessments and audit that decisions were made rationally
They replace the need for solution architecture documents
They are required before any code can be deployed to production
knowledgeCheck.explanation: ADRs provide a clear, dated audit trail showing that decisions were made deliberately with appropriate consideration of alternatives. This evidence is valuable for spend control submissions, service assessment panels, and audit reviews. They are not mandated by the TCoP, do not replace solution architecture documents, and are not a deployment gate.

practicalExercise.title: Retrospective ADR Writing Sprint
practicalExercise.scenario: You've joined a DESNZ programme that's been running for 18 months without any ADRs. The service is a carbon emissions reporting platform used by 5,000 industrial sites. The tech lead is leaving in four weeks. In conversations with the team, you've identified these significant decisions that were never documented: (1) The choice to use a graph database (Neo4j) for modelling relationships between companies, sites, and emission sources. (2) The decision to build a custom calculation engine rather than using an off-the-shelf product. (3) The choice to implement real-time data validation rather than batch processing. (4) The decision to use a single-tenant architecture despite multi-tenancy being cheaper.
practicalExercise.task:
Write two complete ADRs from the list above. For each:

1. Reconstruct the likely context based on the scenario information
2. State the decision clearly
3. Identify plausible alternatives that were probably considered
4. Document realistic consequences (positive and negative)
5. Note that the ADR was written retrospectively and may be incomplete
hints: For the graph database decision, think about why relationships between companies, sites, and sources matter for emissions reporting
For the custom calculation engine, consider the complexity of emissions calculations and how often regulations change
Be honest about what you're inferring vs what you know for certain
Include a note about validating the ADR with the departing tech lead
practicalExercise.modelAnswer:
**ADR-001 (Retrospective): Use Neo4j Graph Database for Entity Relationship Modelling**

Status: Accepted (retrospectively documented)
Note: This ADR was written retrospectively based on team discussions. Some context may be incomplete.

Context: The carbon emissions reporting platform needs to model complex relationships between corporate groups, individual companies, industrial sites, emission sources, and regulatory obligations. A single corporate group might own 50 companies operating 200 sites with 1,000 emission sources, each subject to different regulatory regimes.

Alternatives Considered:
- PostgreSQL with recursive CTEs: Could model hierarchies but complex relationship queries would be slow and hard to maintain.
- Document database (MongoDB): Poor fit for highly relational data with complex traversal requirements.
- Neo4j graph database: Natural fit for relationship-heavy data with variable-depth traversals.

Decision: We use Neo4j as the primary data store for entity relationships and regulatory obligations.

Consequences:
- Positive: Relationship queries are fast and intuitive. Schema flexibility accommodates evolving regulatory structures.
- Negative: Smaller talent pool for Neo4j skills. Less mature backup/recovery tooling. Team needed upskilling.

To validate: Confirm with departing tech lead that performance requirements for relationship traversal were the primary driver.
assessmentCriteria: Acknowledges the retrospective nature and potential incompleteness honestly
Reconstructs plausible context based on available information
Identifies realistic alternatives with credible rejection rationale
Documents both positive and negative consequences
Identifies what needs validation with the departing team member

commonMistakes: Writing ADRs that are too long and detailed, turning a lightweight practice into a heavyweight burden
Only recording the chosen option without documenting alternatives considered and rejected
Writing ADRs as proposals rather than records of decisions already made
Listing only positive consequences, making the ADR look like a sales pitch rather than honest analysis
Storing ADRs in a location separate from the code, making them hard to find and easy to forget
Requiring formal approval workflows that add friction and discourage adoption
Only having the architect write ADRs instead of empowering the whole team
Never reviewing or superseding ADRs, leaving outdated decisions as the official record

weakVsStrong.weak: A weak SA makes architecture decisions in meetings and Slack conversations without recording them. When challenged six months later about why a particular technology was chosen, they struggle to remember the reasoning. When new team members question the approach, the same debates happen again. When the spend control submission asks for evidence of decision-making rigour, the SA has to reconstruct rationale from memory and meeting notes. The architecture appears ad-hoc rather than deliberate.
weakVsStrong.strong: A strong SA writes an ADR within 24 hours of any significant architecture decision. The ADRs are stored in the repository, reviewed in pull requests, and referenced in code comments. When challenged about a decision, they point to the ADR. When new team members join, they read the ADR log as part of onboarding and understand the architecture's evolution within days. When governance asks for evidence, the ADR log demonstrates a clear trail of deliberate, well-reasoned decisions.
